documents.title: Project 33 (topherchris420/33)
documents.text:
Vers3Dynamics | Applied Aerospace Research

A small, inexpensive folding-fin rocket testbed in which every engineering claim is tied to the exact artifacts that support it, the class of evidence those artifacts are, and the measurements still missing.

The rocket is the specimen. The record of how engineering knowledge moves from assumption to model to implementation to measurement is the product.

documents.title: Project 33 — Current status
documents.text:
Project 33 is a bench-validation prototype. It has models, CAD, firmware that compiles, a telemetry dashboard, and automated checks. No physical measurement has been accepted into the evidence record. Nothing here is flight-tested or flight-ready, and live propulsion is outside the repository's validation boundary.

Record state: 8 claims · 3 contradicted · 4 unresolved · 1 supported within stated limits · 0 accepted physical measurements · 17 open discrepancies of 24 · 5 of 5 predictions not measured.

Unresolved is a valid engineering state. Several research claims are currently contradicted by their own models, and saying so is the point.

documents.title: Project 33 — Evidence Observatory
documents.text:
The Evidence Observatory (evidence/, Python standard library only, fully offline) is the centre of the project. For every claim it answers:

- What is claimed? A passport per claim: question, current statement, status, assumptions, limitations.
- What stands behind it, and what kind of evidence is that? Exact files with SHA-256 digests, each classed on an evidence ladder: specification, implementation, test procedure, synthetic, analytical, simulated, software verified, bench observed, bench measured.
- Does it meet its requirements? Machine-checkable requirements are evaluated from committed values and labeled with the evidence class they came from: SATISFIED (analytical) is not SATISFIED (bench measured).
- What disagrees? A discrepancy register of recorded mismatches between models, requirements, documentation, firmware, CAD, and the BOM.
- What is still unknown? Predictions frozen before measurement, shown as NOT MEASURED, never zero.
- What changed, and which reviews are no longer sufficient? Dependency tracking marks a claim's review stale when any file it rests on changes, without declaring the claim false.

Support is derived, never authored: a model cannot become a measurement, synthetic data cannot be relabeled as physical, and no claim can be promoted past a validation gate without a human-accepted inert measurement. The tooling refuses to build a report from a record that tries.

documents.title: Project 33 — The engineering loop
documents.text:
flowchart LR
 Q[Question] --> M[Model] --> P[Registered prediction] --> I[Implementation]
 I --> T[Inert test, pre-registered] --> E[Captured session] --> A[Audit + passport]
 A --> H{Named human accepts?} -->|yes| C[Comparison with prediction] --> R[Claim review] --> Q
 H -->|no| X[Rejected, kept with reason]

Software may propose an inert experiment and check it against machine-readable rules. A human decides whether to perform it. Only the resulting measurement, accepted by a named reviewer, enters the record. Confidence is not authority.

documents.title: Project 33 — What has actually been demonstrated
documents.text:
Only software-level facts, each with a named scope:

- Firmware builds: both PlatformIO projects compile in CI. Compiling is not hardware behavior.
- Software tests: the Python suite passes in CI; CI review packets attach the JUnit run record.
- Model reproduction: every committed model output regenerates from source and matches by value (python -m evidence reproduce).

documents.title: Project 33 — What has not been measured
documents.text: Everything physical. Timing jitter, spring rate, part masses, dry CG, servo authority, gyro drift, current draw, interlock behavior on hardware, mechanism deployment, and stiffness are all NOT MEASURED. Inert experiments are drafted as pre-registrations awaiting adoption by a human (P-001 timing, P-002 spring rate, P-003 drift).

documents.title: Project 33 — Reproduce the review
documents.text:
Python 3.11+, no packages, no network, no hardware:

With the model dependencies installed (pip install -r requirements-evidence.txt), python -m evidence reproduce regenerates every model output in a temporary directory and compares values. make review-full builds a packet with the test and reproduction run records attached.

documents.title: Project 33 — Validation roadmap
documents.text: The project moves only through explicit gates: analytical model → software reproduction → synthetic test → inert bench setup → inert physical measurement → repeated measurement → independent review. Gates from inert bench setup onward need a human-registered pre-registration or a human-accepted measurement. No AI model, CI run, or repository setting can move a claim across them. Next steps are in the Roadmap; the readiness matrix is in Project Status.

documents.title: Project 33 — Safety boundary
documents.text: This repository is for inert bench validation, simulation, and engineering review. Dashboard launch is rejected by default in firmware; the physical arming switch, readiness handshake, heartbeat timeout, and rocket-side arming state all stay in force, and refusals are logged. Automated tools, including AI assistants, may interpret the record; they may not create measurements, accept sessions, or touch any safety gate. See Safety. Field testing is a separate, safety-reviewed process outside this repository.

documents.title: Anna · R.A.I.N. DataMatrix Engine — Why Anna
documents.text:
Commercial search locks institutions in: per-seat SaaS pricing, sensitive documents
leaving your infrastructure, and closed ranking you can't audit. Anna is the opposite —
open infrastructure for knowledge systems:

- Self-host — run the whole stack on your own servers or cloud account; nothing
 routes through a vendor.
- Own your data — every document, embedding, and query stays inside infrastructure
 you control end to end.
- Open source — the full engine (retrieval, ranking, summarization) is public and
 auditable, not a black box.

documents.title: Anna · R.A.I.N. DataMatrix Engine — Features
documents.text:
Capability — Description
Natural-language search — Ask questions in plain English; a local sentence-embedding model powers semantic retrieval.
Hybrid retrieval — BM25 lexical matching fused with dense-vector kNN via Reciprocal Rank Fusion.
Inspectable source reports — Query-matching excerpts with exact source offsets; explicit refusal when evidence is absent; model citation checks with extractive fallback.
Retrieval explanations — See which retrievers ran, each result’s ranks and score contributions, and when vector search uses hashing or degrades to lexical search.
Verifiable research records — Export the current query, results, and cited excerpts as Markdown or versioned JSON with a deterministic SHA-256 content fingerprint — then re-verify any saved record later: the engine recomputes the fingerprint and re-reads every cited passage from the current index, from the workbench, the CLI, or the API.
Citations for every document — BibTeX entries and plain-text references, deterministic and byte-identical from the workbench (Live or Demo), the server pages, GET /api/v1/document//citation and flask engine cite. The Markdown report ends with a keyed References section, and the page's bibliography saves as .bib.
Document comparison — Side-by-side comparison of two documents by shared terms, categories, and similarity.
Code and equation search — Detects source code and LaTeX, so results can be filtered to reference code, datasheets, and standards.
PDF indexing — Extracts and indexes text from PDFs (arXiv, NASA, DOE, NIST).
Version-aware documentation — Captures documentation versions (for example ESP-IDF v5.1, Linux kernel v6.6) for precise filtering.
Faceted filtering — Filter by source, type, category, language, version, code/equations, and year.
Related recommendations — "More like this" for any document: vector neighbours with a semantic model, shared title terms otherwise.
REST API — Everything the UI does is available as JSON under /api/v1.
Collections and bookmarks — Save documents into named collections (PostgreSQL).
Plugin architecture — Add a new knowledge source in a single file.

Inspect the evidence:

Search → open Why this result? → click a citation to inspect the original
passage → save the research record as Markdown or JSON → later, **File ▸ Verify
research record…** (or flask engine verify-record) recomputes its fingerprint
and re-reads every cited passage from the current index, reporting each one as
verified, relocated, drifted or missing. Source excerpts and model-written
answers are labeled separately; a valid citation number does not establish
factual support. See the evidence contract.

Cite what you found:

Details on any result ends with its citation — a BibTeX entry
(@article{devlin2024zero, …}) and a one-line reference, each one Copy away —
and Save references .bib writes the whole result page as a bibliography.
The entries are deterministic: the same document gives the same key and the
same bytes from the workbench, the server pages, the API and the CLI
(engine/citations.py and frontend/citations.js are byte-exact twins, kept
in step by a test that runs the JavaScript under Node). Each entry carries an
annaid field, the engine's document id, so a reference traces back to the
index it came from.

documents.title: Anna · R.A.I.N. DataMatrix Engine — Architecture
documents.text:
The engine/ package is framework-agnostic and imports every heavy dependency
lazily, so the application boots even without the machine-learning stack —
falling back to a deterministic embedder and metadata-only indexing. Full design
notes are in docs/ARCHITECTURE.md.

The server-rendered pages at / and the static workbench are two faces of one
contract: an unreachable index is reported as an outage, never as an empty
result; relevance is one 0–1 scale everywhere; retrieval modes are named for
what the connected backend actually runs (Postgres full-text search is not
BM25, and term-hashing vectors are not semantic); every hit explains its rank;
and every document can be cited.

documents.title: CIRCLE (topherchris420/circle)
documents.text:
Close the loop. Keep the evidence.

An open research test bench for physiological sensing, adaptive feedback, and human authority.

Run a session · Follow the evidence · Test the limits · Human authority · Explore the project · Contribute

One simulated session. Several physiological pathways. Every decision on the same timeline.
Ground truth is available to the evaluator; the controller works from device records alone.

When a system senses a change and responds, what would let another researcher trust the record?

CIRCLE makes that question runnable. It reconstructs physiological signals from simulated sensor codes, decides when haptic guidance is warranted, and preserves the evidence from the original samples through the observed cue. An independent auditor then rebuilds the session from its raw bundle.

The research ambition is a closed-loop human-state platform whose actions remain inspectable, reproducible, and subject to meaningful consent. Today, you can run the digital test bench, challenge its controller, audit its decisions, and examine a standalone cryptographic consent gate. The hardware is a design awaiting physical validation.

Warning: ENGINEERING REVIEW ONLY. Experimental research hardware and software. This repository is not approved for fabrication or human connection and does not establish medical-device, electrical-safety, EMC, or measurement-performance claims. All physiological results shown here come from simulation.

documents.title: CIRCLE — Quick start
documents.text:
Run your first session:

You need Python 3.11+, Git, and the dependencies in requirements.txt. No device, account, API key, or model server is required for the simulation.

git clone https://github.com/topherchris420/circle.git
cd circle
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python tools/run_physiology_twin.py --output outputs/physiology --audit

Prefer an isolated Python environment?:

After cloning and entering circle, create a virtual environment with python -m venv .venv. Activate it with source .venv/bin/activate on macOS/Linux or .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 in Windows PowerShell, then run the install and experiment commands above. If your system names Python python3, use that command instead.

The default run simulates six minutes: rest, breath hold, a stressor, and recovery with adaptive haptic guidance. It also runs a matched sham arm for comparison, exports the session, scores estimates against hidden truth, and audits the exported evidence.

Open the report and follow one decision:

Open outputs/physiology/report.html in your browser. The report is self-contained: zoom the traces, open a row in the decision ledger, and follow its evidence down to the source samples.

Question — Where to look
What did the controller know at that moment? — Input cutoff, availability times, features, and exact sample ranges
Why did it act—or hold? — Controller state, formula components, and quality-gate outcomes
Did the cue occur? — Command, electrical onset, and IMU-observed vibration
What changes when cues are withheld? — Matched sham traces, under the twin's assumed response model
Can the record be reconstructed? — Decision replay and independent audit verdict

A successful reconstruction reports REPLAY_MATCH. That establishes agreement between the export and reconstruction from its inputs. The simulation scorecard separately measures agreement with the twin's truth.

To explore before running anything, open the committed example report locally after cloning. The image above is a static preview of that interface.

Know what the run preserves:

Export — Purpose
raw/*.csv.gz — Sensor codes and timing records used for reconstruction
session.ndjson — Versioned device and derived records, lineage, gaps, and intervention chains
closed_loop_ledger.json — Every controller evaluation and the evidence it read
analysis.json · scorecard.json — Recovered estimates and checks against simulated truth
truth.json · counterfactual.json — Evaluator truth and the matched opposite arm; never controller inputs
manifest.json · passport.txt — Configuration, software provenance, artifact hashes, and session summary
report.html — Interactive view of the traces, decisions, scorecard, and execution evidence

The pipeline methods explain how each channel and metric is derived.

documents.title: CIRCLE — How CIRCLE works
documents.text:
The central question is what gives this system grounds to act?

A rise in heart rate is one observation. A rise in skin conductance is another. CIRCLE requires agreement across the cardiovascular and electrodermal pathways, sufficient signal quality, and a sustained observed state before guidance can begin.

Stage — Evidence CIRCLE preserves
Observe — Raw skin conductance (EDA), optical pulse (PPG), motion (IMU), and synchronization records; device times, sequence numbers, availability, and declared gaps
Infer — Recovered physiological features, with lineage to the exact samples used
Decide — State, input cutoff, formula components, and explicit outcomes for acting, holding, or stopping
Intervene — The scheduled command, electrical onset, and vibration detected from IMU samples
Reconstruct — Analysis and derived records rebuilt from raw inputs, followed by an explicit replay verdict

Three rules make the loop inspectable:

- A decision can use only evidence available at the time. A sample must have been available by the decision time and been taken at or before the input cutoff. FIFO stalls, delayed delivery, and missing samples remain visible in the record.
- Holding is a decision. Motion, poor contact, stale data, or disagreeing pathways can prevent guidance. After impairment, the controller requires a full clean 40-second evidence window before treating an elevated state as sustained; repeated quality loss during guidance stops it.
- Each stage earns its own evidence. A command does not prove vibration, and vibration does not establish a physiological effect. PHYSICALLY_OBSERVED requires an observation record; in this test bench, that observation is simulated too.

The pipeline and controller consume the shared RawSession boundary without importing hidden truth. The auditor reconstructs derived records instead of accepting their stored values. A derived record that disagrees with reconstruction remains detectable even if its checksums are rewritten; hashes alone do not authenticate the underlying data.

Replay names its result: REPLAY_MATCH, REPLAY_DIVERGENCE, TIMING_VIOLATION, VERSION_MISMATCH, EVIDENCE_INTEGRITY_FAILURE, MISSING_SOURCE, or INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE.

Read the evidence contract and failure history, record schema, and auditor.

documents.title: CIRCLE — Test the failure modes
documents.text:
Change the conditions, then inspect whether the controller's behavior is justified:

The scenario suite tests both sides of the decision: refusing unwarranted guidance and acting when a warranted state becomes observable. A controller that always holds cannot pass. The scenario definitions specify each disturbance and judge the result against hidden truth.

To inspect a deliberate loss of measurement quality, export the poor-contact scenario:

python tools/run_physiology_twin.py --scenario poor_contact --output outputs/poor-contact --audit

With the default seed 7, this run withholds guidance, passes 14 of 19 scorecard checks, and returns exit code 1 because five checks fail. Its audit still reports REPLAY_MATCH: the impaired session can be reconstructed faithfully. Measurement quality and evidence integrity answer different questions. Open outputs/poor-contact/report.html to examine both.

The twin assumes that paced breathing changes its simulated physiology. Active-versus-sham comparisons test the software under that assumption; a physiological effect in people would need separate evidence.

documents.title: Mannahatta (topherchris420/cognisync-terrain-weaver)
documents.text:
The land remembers. The city is not finished.

A counterfactual urban resilience instrument: examine what a place was, model what happens when rain meets its present surfaces, and ask what would have to change.

What was. What is. What could be. The map is the workspace; the score is the beginning of the question.

This is a reproducible calculation, not a measured site outcome or a screenshot. A hypothetical 1,000 m² paved site under 50 mm rainfall generates 44 m³ of bulk runoff. Converting half to trees and half to bioswales produces 7.5 m³ under the same fixed-coefficient model, at an assumed installation cost of $55,000. The map-based workflow additionally routes water over terrain; these two calculations are deliberately separate.

documents.title: Mannahatta — Start with a place
documents.text:
1. Open the map and choose Explore an example. The fixture works without an AI classification request; its status stays visible in exports.
2. In Overview, inspect the composition, historical reconstruction where available, and vegetation–pavement sensitivity. Live scans also expose the captured imagery.
3. In Storm, choose rainfall and resolution, then route a one-hour design event. Its forcing is sealed for the comparison.
4. In Mitigation, ask Catalyst what a target and budget permit. Then draw supported interventions on the actual study extent.
5. Rerun the sealed storm and compare NOW / POSSIBLE with the synchronized map view. Then read where the water moved: the cells that carry less water on the redesigned surface, the drawing's own footprint on the grid, and how far downstream the change reaches.
6. Export the study or its experiment evidence JSON, including inputs, drawings, coefficients, forcing, routed results and the spatial difference. Open an experiment file reopens it: every identity is verified and the pair is routed again by the running build before anything is shown.

Live imagery, historical rasters and elevation require their external services. If elevation cannot load, a deterministic slope is explicitly illustrative. Example land cover never becomes a measurement merely because the terrain loaded successfully.

documents.title: Mannahatta — Three questions, different evidence
documents.text:
Frame — What it contains — What it does not establish
1609 — what was — Welikia ecological reconstruction reduced to block bounding boxes where coverage exists; a separately labeled island-wide reference score of 79.1 — Surveyed historical boundaries, a complete settlement history, or the history of an arbitrary block outside coverage
Present — what is — Captured imagery, inferred five-class land cover and deterministically derived score — A surveyed surface map, measured infiltration or validated flood probability
Possible — what could be — Interventions evaluated with the same coefficients and, for routed pairs, the same storm and terrain — A forecast, construction approval or prediction of political adoption

Beneath all three sits a fourth question: how do we know? Overview lists every component — reconstruction, classification, score, coefficients, elevation, routing, interventions — with the kind of number it produces and how far it has been tested, generated from the committed experiments rather than written by hand.

Mannahatta's historical frame concerns land inhabited and shaped by the Lenape. An ecology reconstruction is not an account of empty or untouched land. The written five-class benchmark is this application's estimate informed by the Mannahatta/Welikia descriptions, not a five-class dataset published by WCS. The reconstructed block index is a different source and must retain its own transformation notes.

documents.title: Mannahatta — What would have to change?
Mannahatta — What if the classification is wrong?
documents.text:
The land-cover classifier is the largest measured uncertainty source. Its outputs are coarse: 82% of stored class values are multiples of 5. They are unstable: one frame classified 24 times received 15 different compositions, with water anywhere from 0 to 45% and pervious share spanning 29 percentage points (C2). Against the independent USGS NLCD 2021 map, pervious share differs by 6.7 points on average across 16 frames (C1).

Overview offers a bounded experiment: transfer percentage points between vegetation and pavement, preserving the other classes and total area, and see the pavement, score and 50 mm bulk-runoff range. The default range is benchmark-derived (±7 pp); the repeat-run range (±15 pp) or a chosen what-if are alternatives. Transfers stop when a source class runs out. It leaves the stored analysis untouched.

This is sensitivity analysis, not a statistical confidence interval. It does not quantify every source of error, and NLCD has its own. The shared input contract rejects incomplete, negative, non-finite or materially unbalanced compositions before accepting classifier/MCP percentages. Scores are computed by code, not accepted from a model narrative.

metadata.section: What if the classification is wrong?

documents.title: Mannahatta — Two water models, explicit limits
documents.text:
Bulk land budget:

The score is a weighted screening index normalized over land:

score = 100 × Σ(land-cover share × retention weight) / total land share

Class — Retention weight
Vegetation — 0.80
Bare soil — 0.70
Buildings — 0.10
Pavement — 0.12
Open water — Excluded from the land denominator

Scenario costs and water volumes use physical land area, excluding open water. The rainfall workbench compares 10, 25, 50, 100 and 200 mm, with a continuous 0–200 mm control and an accessible table. For every depth, retained volume + runoff = rain on land.

Fixed coefficients yield linear responses: this model cannot identify saturation or a storm intensity at which an intervention stops working. Its rainfall presets are exploratory depths, not sourced return periods.

Terrain routing:

The browser loads Terrarium elevation onto a finite grid and routes water with D8 over static fill-and-spill (routing v2): closed depressions hold up to their volume and spill the rest, and cells at or below 0 m are treated as receiving tidal water. The original D8 stranded a median 81% of routed water in single-cell pits and in Terrarium artefacts as deep as −14 km; the analytic pit and flat cases now pass (R1, R2). Intervention modifiers are weighted by the share of each cell a drawing covers, so credited area no longer depends on resolution. A synthetic slope is used and labeled if elevation is unavailable. NOW and POSSIBLE share rainfall, duration, resolution and elevation identity; edited futures invalidate the previous comparison. Surface identities include study bounds and classified cover.

A controlled pair is also subtracted cell by cell. The difference layer colours the cells through which the redesigned surface sends less water (and any through which it sends more), outlines the drawing's own cells, and reports how far downstream the change reaches; the ledger beside it keeps the avoided runoff, because water is counted at every cell it passes. A pair that differs in anything but the drawn surface has no difference layer, only a list of what differs. Like every routed quantity, it shows where this model sends water, not where flooding becomes less likely.

Routed zones did not locate reported flooding. …

documents.title: Dynamic Resonance Rooting (topherchris420/dynamic-resonance-rooting)
documents.text:
Measure the rhythm. Trace the lag. Keep the evidence.

Dynamic Resonance Rooting (DRR) is an open-source Python research framework for multivariate time series. It looks for oscillatory structure, estimates lagged relationships between signals, measures resonance depth, and surfaces structural change diagnostics with explicit provenance and review boundaries.

The outputs are diagnostics. A directed edge is a statistical lead–lag relationship under a chosen estimator and null model; it does not establish causation. A result in one domain does not automatically generalize to another.

The layers are DRR core → validation substrate → domain adapters. The core contains numerical operators. The validation substrate tests specifications, synthetic ground truth, leakage and preregistered external evidence. Domain adapters scope a method to a particular application; sharing an operator never transfers an evidence claim from one domain to another.

Start here: Run the synthetic example · Inspect the evidence · Try the live lab · Choose a workflow · Read the architecture

documents.title: Dynamic Resonance Rooting — A rhythm is not yet a reason
documents.text:
A time series can offer a compelling story and still be wrong. DRR treats that moment as the start of an investigation, not its conclusion.

Ask — Test — Resist the temptation to claim
What repeats? — Spectral peaks and resonance depth under an explicit noise reference — A detected frequency is a mechanism
What tends to precede what? — Lag search against a surrogate null whose assumption is named and measured, with multiple-test control — A directed statistical edge is causation
What changed? — State-space and structural-change methods under a declared holdout and false-alarm budget — An alarm on one dataset generalizes to another
Does the tool itself behave? — Known-injection fixtures, calibration trials and adversarial counterexamples — Synthetic success proves external utility

An experiment worth trying: run the synthetic quick start, where the correct lag is known. Then read the NOAA QBO external comparison, where the preregistered structural-change claim was not supported. Holding both results in view is the point of the project: an instrument should preserve its successes and the data that contradicts its ambitions.

metadata.section: A rhythm is not yet a reason

documents.title: Dynamic Resonance Rooting — What it does
documents.text:
Question — DRR component — What you get
Which rhythms recur, and for how long? — FFT, Welch, wavelet, and resonance-depth operators — Frequencies, spectral power, and depth components
Which signal tends to lead another? — Lagged correlation or transfer entropy against a circular-shift, phase-randomization, or permutation null — Candidate edges, tested edges, lags, and p-values
Has the system's structure shifted? — State-space, topology, and structural-surprise diagnostics — Estimated states, changes, and uncertainty to investigate
Can a bounded input change a simulated state? — Navigation engine and matched control experiments — Proposed interventions and comparison metrics for a modeled system

The core operates on a numeric series. The validation substrate includes synthetic ground truth, specification and leakage tests, surrogate inference, and a preregistered external comparison. The domain adapters apply the same core to specific workflows, such as physics, sensing, macro policy, banking supervision, or typed judgment. A universal claim is about the operators; a domain claim stays in the adapter.

documents.title: Dynamic Resonance Rooting — Quick start
documents.text:
Use Python 3.8 or newer. For a checkout of the current code:

git clone https://github.com/topherchris420/dynamic-resonance-rooting.git
cd dynamic-resonance-rooting
python -m pip install -e .

This example generates three synthetic channels: a 12.5 Hz source, a copy delayed by two samples, and an independent distractor. It then runs the spectral, depth, and rooting operators. The random seed keeps the example deterministic.

On the checked synthetic fixture, the selected edge is dim_0 → dim_1 at lag 2. candidate_edges are exploratory; significant_edges pass the selected surrogate test and correction. With 25 surrogates, the check is stable and reproducible.

For the packaged, deterministic benchmark without writing output files:

drr-reproduce --no-artifacts

Or run the complete example and write JSON/CSV artifacts to a directory you choose:

drr-reproduce --output-dir results/reproduction

documents.title: Dynamic Resonance Rooting — What the evidence says
documents.text:
The synthetic oscillator checks whether the implementation recovers known, injected frequency and lag. It is a specification check, not evidence of general predictive performance.

A Monte Carlo calibration study measures the statistical behavior of the operators on simulated systems where the answer is known. Its artifact is regenerated with python scripts/run_calibration_study.py.

Question — Measured answer (512 samples, 99 surrogates, α = 0.05)
Does the rooting test keep its false-alarm rate? — Yes. Family-wise error is 0.040–0.062 on independent AR(1) series from white noise to 0.97. The legacy permutation null reaches 0.97 and is only for serially independent data.
Does it find real lead–lag edges? — A 0.3 coupling is recovered in 99.5% of trials, 0.2 in 66%. Strong memory in every channel lowers power and makes the target appear to lead its source.
Is resonance depth a test? — No. It separates a clear tone from white noise, but red noise at AR 0.9 scores above a −9 dB tone. Compare it against a surrogate or red-noise reference.
Does the null survive long memory? — While the series are stationary, yes. The default circular-shift null measures 0.048–0.060 on fractional Gaussian noise from white noise to Hurst 0.95 and 0.055 on GARCH(1,1) noise; the permutation null reaches 0.797 at Hurst 0.95. On a random walk every null fails (0.27–0.89), so difference or detrend nonstationary series first.

The last row is a second preregistered study, and it asks the question the method itself depends on: which null assumptions keep lag-search false alarms controlled when the noise never forgets? Six hypotheses were fixed before the run, two of them predicting the method's own failure, and all six were supported. The study record has the protocol and every row; its artifact is regenerated with python scripts/run_dependent_noise_study.py.

The repository also contains a preregistered external comparison on the NOAA CPC quasi-biennial oscillation series. Its reviewed machine-readable artifact records the current claim as not supported (not_supported): the full DRR holdout false-alarm rate exceeds the preregistered tolerance. This result is specific to the equatorial stratospheric zonal-wind comparison and does not establish results in other domains.

To reproduce that comparison from the vendored public-data snapshots:

python scripts/run_structural_change_benchmark.py --output-dir results/expected

The protocol fixes the dataset checksums, disruption windows, holdout, baselines, ablations, tolerance, and decision rule. The review memo explains the evidence and current conclusion.

documents.title: Dynamic Resonance Rooting — Live lab
documents.text: Open index.html in a browser to run DRR on a streaming three-channel system whose truth you set: coupling, delay, rhythm, and noise. Each 512-sample window is analyzed in the page by drr-engine.js, a port of the Python operators that tests/test_web_engine_parity.py checks against this package to 1e-9. The lab keeps a running count of recovered edges, misses, and false alarms, so you can watch the test hold its 5% rate when you cut the link. Below it, every evidence chart is drawn from the committed artifacts, including the null-model study and the external result that went against us.

documents.text:

Five scenarios: accepted steering · replayed sequence · conflicting pedals · stale command · expired command lease. Compare the fictional ASTER, VECTOR, and NOMAD vehicle profiles. The diagram is an educational illustration of documented rules, not a live connection to the simulator or a real vehicle.

documents.title: ghostwheel — The interesting part is the refusal
documents.text:
Imagine asking a car to turn right.

The instruction arrives. A gateway inspects who sent it, when it was issued, whether it has already been used, and whether the requested motion fits the model's limits. The command may pass. It may be rejected. Either way, something observable happens next.

GHOSTWHEEL lets you investigate that moment.

Instead of showing a green light and asking you to trust it, the laboratory exposes the command verdict, virtual actuator response, synthetic telemetry, recorded events, and evidence you can inspect again. It is a small, deliberately bounded world built to make cyber-physical reasoning visible.

Discover → Drive → Experiment → Investigate → Understand.

documents.title: ghostwheel — Your first investigation
documents.text:
Five minutes. One virtual vehicle. One question worth answering.

Step — Do this — Discover this
01 / DISCOVER — Launch the lab, open Operations, and choose ASTER. — The vehicle has a modeled architecture, telemetry, and an authorization boundary.
02 / DRIVE — Select Enable controls. Hold W to accelerate; steer with A / D; use S to brake. — Requested steering and modeled steering are not necessarily the same.
03 / EXPERIMENT — Under Test a safeguard, choose REPLAY / duplicate sequence and select Run scenario. — The gateway rejects a reused command with the reason replayed_sequence.
04 / INVESTIGATE — Select Finish drive & review, inspect integrity, then choose Save recording or Export verification ledger. — A result is more useful when you can follow its event trail.
05 / UNDERSTAND — Open Research lab, set a seed, and run the experiment suite. — The same test meets three different modeled vehicle architectures.

Controls: Hold W to accelerate, S to brake, A / D to steer, and press Space to request a virtual Safe Stop. Hold-and-release buttons also work. Keep the app window focused. The in-app Quick start and four-step walkthrough guide the same first investigation.

Operations starts with a focused driving view. Select Show technical instruments for precision sliders, steering response, synthetic CAN messages, ECU health, and command events. Your view preference is remembered on this device. Opening replay stops the driving controls and pauses the live simulation; use Return to simulator, then Resume simulation to continue. Walkthrough progress belongs to the current run and survives leaving replay.

Nothing in that sequence requires a real car, a CAN adapter, ROS 2, or CARLA.

documents.title: ghostwheel — The fleet
documents.text:
Three fictional electric vehicles. Three ways for a command to become motion.

Vehicle — Teaching architecture — What makes it interesting
ASTER / compact EV — A central gateway and one modeled steering ECU; 2.65 m wheelbase. — Start here. Explore basic steering lag, validation, and virtual safe-state behavior.
VECTOR / touring EV — Two steering channels with slightly different response rates; 2.96 m wheelbase. — Examine channel disagreement and a modeled monitor that reacts beyond a 2° difference.
NOMAD / utility EV — A zonal teaching profile and slower steering actuator; 3.25 m wheelbase. — See why an identical instruction can trace a different path through a longer, slower model.

Change vehicles. Repeat a test. Compare the response.

These are original, simplified models with invented parameters, virtual ECU names, and synthetic CAN frames. They are not digital twins of commercial vehicles, validated OEM calibrations, or firmware emulators. The point is to understand how assumptions change outcomes, not to rank real cars by security.

documents.title: ghostwheel — GW-01 concept blueprint
documents.text:
The invisible decision, made visible. Explore a high-level CAD-style
interpretation of ASTER's virtual chassis, command gateway, synthetic
telemetry, software ECUs, and recorded evidence.

Explore the assembly: Editable 3D OpenSCAD model
· Full blueprint notes
· Engineering architecture

This is a conceptual research illustration, not a physical vehicle
controller or build-ready automotive CAD model. ASTER's 2.65 m wheelbase
comes from the simulator; the rest of the geometry is illustrative.
No browser or desktop control path reaches real steering, throttle, or
brakes.

documents.title: ghostwheel — The gateway
documents.text:
Every request has to earn its way to a simulated actuator.

Before a control reaches the model, GHOSTWHEEL checks its structure, session and capability, vehicle scope, sequence number, simulation timestamp, value ranges, conflicting pedals, steering slew, and a simplified lateral-acceleration envelope.

Consider two requests:

Request — Gateway decision — Modeled consequence
A fresh, authorized steering request inside the model's limits — authorized — The virtual actuator begins responding, with its own lag and rate limit.
Throttle 0.8 and brake 0.8 in one command — conflicting_pedals — The command is rejected, a virtual safe state is requested, and the event is recorded.

A repeated sequence produces replayed_sequence. An old simulation timestamp produces stale_command. The fault explorer also covers invalid credentials, future timestamps, out-of-range demands, implausible steering jumps, malformed envelopes, and dropped heartbeats.

The built-in world advances in 50 ms simulation steps. Its six-tick command lease triggers a modeled watchdog stop on the seventh tick, 350 ms of simulated time after the last accepted control tick. This is not a wall-clock guarantee, physical stopping distance, or safety-rated intervention.

The connector registry enforces another boundary: application actuation transports must be simulation-only. Physical CAN, OBD, serial, and remote-device actuation connectors are rejected by design. See the implementation and the trust model.

documents.title: ghostwheel — The laboratory
documents.text:
Don't just trigger a fault. Make it measurable.

The Research lab runs a seeded experiment suite across ASTER, VECTOR, and NOMAD. Each architecture has a baseline trajectory, eight finite invalid-command trials, and a separate missing-heartbeat trial.

You can inspect:

- Gateway verdicts: what was accepted or rejected, and why.
- Steering tracking RMSE: how the modeled actuator followed the requested angle.
- Gateway processing time: local software validation and state-application timing, not network latency or real actuator timing.
- Watchdog outcomes and assertions: what the finite scenarios actually checked, including failures.
- Exported report JSON: the seed, per-architecture results, and measured totals.

Try seed 42, then run another seed. Compare ASTER with VECTOR. Ask whether a different steering response changed the experiment's conclusion.

The suite is repeatable; it is not an exhaustive attack test. Measurements describe this implementation and its synthetic models, not real-world vehicle safety or an OEM vulnerability.

documents.title: hello_os (topherchris420/ideas)
documents.text:
hello_os is a compact, importable Python package for exploring safe
gravitomagnetic rotor-array toy models, synthetic detector traces, and
configuration-driven optimization.

The repository now separates supported code from the original Colab export:

- hello_os/ contains the maintained Python package and CLI.
- test_hello_os.py exercises the real package surface.
- explainer/ holds an animated explainer video for the model.
- legacy/hello_os_colab_export.txt preserves the raw notebook export as
 reference material only. It is intentionally not imported or auto-executed.

documents.title: hello_os — Explainer Video
documents.text:
A six-scene animated explainer walks through the idea, the materials, the safety
model, and the detector trace — all driven by the same numbers the package
computes.

Its data (materials, the safe-tip-speed formula, and the seeded detector trace)
mirrors hello_os/core.py, so the story stays true to the code. The clip above
is a rendered capture of the full 34.5-second animation; see
explainer/ for the interactive source (with live color/material
tweaks) and instructions to run it locally.

documents.title: hello_os — Install
documents.text:
python -m pip install -e ".[dev]"

The supported package depends on NumPy. The development extra installs pytest
for the test suite.

documents.title: hello_os — Use The CLI
documents.text:
python -m hello_os --json
python -m hello_os --material "Silicon Nitride" --rpm 32000 --rotors 24
python -m hello_os --optimize --optimizer-samples 5 --json
python -m hello_os --list-materials
python -m hello_os --sweep rpm --sweep-start 8000 --sweep-stop 36000 --sweep-points 8
python -m hello_os --sensitivity --json
python -m hello_os --svg trace.svg

The CLI emits either readable text or JSON for downstream notebooks, dashboards,
and automation. --sweep varies one design parameter across a range and reports
the best candidate that stays within the stress constraint. --sensitivity
prints log-log elasticities showing how strongly each parameter drives SNR and
rotor stress. --svg PATH writes a dependency-free SVG chart of the sweep (or,
without --sweep, the synthetic trace).

documents.title: hello_os — Use The API
documents.text:
from hello_os import RotorDesign, estimate_rotor_metrics, simulate_trace

design = RotorDesign(
 material_name="Carbon Composite",
 mass_kg=250,
 radius_m=0.7,
 rpm=28_000,
 rotor_count=16,
)

metrics = estimate_rotor_metrics(design)
trace = simulate_trace(design, samples=1000, rng=42)

print(metrics.safety_label)
print(metrics.snr_per_second)
print(trace.trace_m_s2.shape)

Sweeps, Sensitivity, And Charts:

sweep_rotor evaluates metrics along one design axis; sensitivity_report
computes local log-log elasticities, so power-law scalings come out exact
(SNR scales as rpm1, radius_m2, detector_distance_m**-3, ...).
The SVG renderers in hello_os.visualization use only the standard library —
no matplotlib dependency — and are loaded lazily, so import hello_os stays
lightweight.

documents.title: hello_os — Quality Checks
documents.text:
python -m py_compile hello_os/*.py
python -m pytest -q

Before opening a pull request, run the checks above for any files you touched.
The tests are designed to catch numerical edge cases, shape regressions, and CLI
output drift.

documents.title: hello_os — Design Notes
documents.text:
- The package is import-safe: importing hello_os does not start plots,
 installers, network calls, GPU setup, or long simulations.
- Numerical routines validate shapes and finite values before computing.
- Synthetic noise accepts a seed or numpy.random.Generator for reproducible
 experiments.
- The optimizer is a bounded deterministic grid search, so it works without
 SciPy and is predictable in CI.

documents.title: IONS-X Deep Emergence Lab (topherchris420/ions-x-deep-emergence-lab)
documents.text:
A reproducible sandbox for asking whether collective sensing can recover structure in a changing field—and what remains when that structure is removed.

Preview: actual 80-frame run with 40 agents on a 32×32 field, seed 42.

IONS-X places moving sensing agents inside a four-channel field. Agents retain observations, measure rolling correlations, and contribute to a shared, decaying association graph. You can watch a run, analyze sensor CSVs, or run paired synthetic experiments without rendering a single frame.

The useful question is not simply “did a pattern appear?” It is “does the detector respond differently when the injected coupling is absent?” The paired control study makes that question executable.

This is exploratory simulation software from Vers3Dynamics. Its outputs are associations, not demonstrations of causality, consciousness, or nonlocal effects. “Confidence” in legacy exports means absolute Pearson correlation, not statistical confidence. See experiment design and limitations.

documents.title: IONS-X Deep Emergence Lab — Start with one experiment
documents.text:
git clone https://github.com/topherchris420/ions-x-deep-emergence-lab.git
cd ions-x-deep-emergence-lab
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate # Windows PowerShell: .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python -m pip install -e .

ions-x --quick --seed 42 --live

Open outputs/latest.html. The adjacent outputs/latest.metrics.json records detections, unique channel pairs, the effective configuration, code identity, dependency versions, and seed.

The animation shows the channel-0 field, a stable undirected graph, and the observation log. Edge width follows the current decayed correlation weight. The renderer and headless mode use the same simulation engine; rendering does not add extra observations.

documents.title: IONS-X Deep Emergence Lab — Ask what survives the control
documents.text:
ions-x --quick --control-study 8 --frames 100 --agents 40 --field-res 32 \
 --seed 42 --output outputs/control-study.json

For each seed, the engine runs two arms:

Coupled field — Uncoupled field
Channel 1 contributes to channel 0 continuously. — This contribution is disabled.
Channel 2 contributes to channel 3 during coherence windows. — This contribution is disabled.
Seeded initialization, diffusion, nonlinear dynamics, moderator events, and agent movements. — The same initialization, dynamics, events, and movements.

Open outputs/control-study.html for the portable experiment report: all six pairs, per-seed effects, observed ranges, and the effective configuration. It works offline and needs no server. The adjacent JSON is the machine-readable evidence record.

The JSON report contains each paired run, per-pair detection rates, and the mean and range of paired differences. A detection rate is detections divided by eligible agent-windows for that pair. It is not a probability of a true relationship. Agents and overlapping windows are dependent; the report deliberately does not turn their count into a sample size for a significance test.

A checked eight-seed example includes the complete report and observed detection rates.

This is a coupling ablation benchmark for the synthetic model. It is distinct from --preset baseline, which analyzes independent Gaussian channel series with a heuristic threshold. Neither is a validated null model for arbitrary empirical data.

documents.title: IONS-X Deep Emergence Lab — Run without rendering
documents.text:
ions-x --quick --headless --frames 200 --seed 42 --output outputs/run.json

Headless mode writes one JSON report and skips Matplotlib rendering. It is useful for batch work and reproducibility checks. The report distinguishes repeated detections from unique associations and records the actual number of processed frames. Its evaluation section records eligible agent-windows and all six detection rates. Runs shorter than the correlation window are labeled insufficient_observations, with null rates; zero detections after evaluation remain numeric zero.

import ions_x_deep_emergence as lab

result = lab.main([
 "--quick", "--headless", "--frames", "100",
 "--seed", "42", "--output", "outputs/experiment.json",
])
print(result.summary_path)

CLI and main() calls reset configuration before applying options, so a previous experiment cannot silently change the next one. The lower-level SimulationEngine API uses the module configuration and RNG: configure once, then run sequentially. Concurrent engines are not supported.

documents.title: IONS-X Deep Emergence Lab — Analyze sensor telemetry
documents.text:
ions-x --preset empirical --input-data telemetry.csv --headless \
 --output outputs/telemetry.json

Channel — Canonical input — Selected aliases
0: EM / RF — em_rf — magnetometer, rf_noise, rf_spectrum_noise, channel_0
1: Optical / IR — optical_ir — pixel_variance, sky_pixel_variance, ir_anomaly, channel_1
2: REG proxy — consciousness_proxy — reg_variance, reg_entropy, egg_variance, channel_2
3: Reference — Generated locally — Independent Gaussian series in empirical mode

All three measured channels must contain numeric data. Missing or wholly unusable channels and infinite sensor/covariate values are rejected. Partial gaps retain the legacy offline forward-fill/backward-fill behavior, with imputed sensor-cell counts in the report. Optional covariates are kp_index, lunar_phase, sidereal_time, and xray_flux; absent covariates default to zero and are listed in the report.

An optional timestamp column accepts timestamp, time, datetime, date_time, or utc_timestamp. Missing/invalid timestamps are filled, or replaced with a synthetic minute index when none are valid. Input ordering is preserved. Rows are steps; elapsed timestamp gaps do not change the dynamics.

Empirical processing spatializes standardized series onto synthetic bases. It is an offline exploration, with full-series normalization and backward filling that can use future rows. It is not a causal online estimator. The environmental moderator equations are modeling assumptions, not validated physical relationships.

Runs also export longitudinal_run_.csv.gz and metadata_.json beside the requested output. Requests longer than the input are clamped to available rows and report the actual frame count. The passport includes the input file's SHA-256 and preprocessing information.

documents.title: IONS-X Deep Emergence Lab — Choose a configuration
documents.text:
ions-x --experiment coherence --seed 123 --output outputs/coherence.html
ions-x --quick --output outputs/demo.gif
ions-x --preset baseline --headless --frames 100 --output outputs/baseline.json

Flag — Purpose
--quick — 50 agents, 64×64 field, 60 frames; explicit numeric flags override these values.
--experiment NAME — balanced, quick, arv, coherence, or dense-agents.
--frames N, --agents N, --field-res N — Positive integer runtime settings.
--seed N — NumPy RandomState seed, 0 through 4294967295.
--headless — JSON report without animation.
--control-study N — N paired seeds beginning at --seed; synthetic only, JSON plus an offline HTML report.
--preset MODE — synthetic, empirical, or baseline.
--input-data PATH — CSV telemetry; supplying a CSV without a preset is labeled empirical.
--output PATH — .html / .gif for animation, .json for headless or paired study.
--fps N — GIF playback frame rate; default 20.
--live — Stream progress for individual runs.
--show — Display the saved animation in an IPython notebook.
--no-metrics-sidecar — Omit the extra animation summary; headless/study JSON remains the primary output.

Experiment — Active differences from balanced
balanced — 300 agents, 128×128 field, 500 frames; 50-observation correlation window, threshold 0.32.
quick — 50 agents, 64×64 field, 60 frames.
arv — Memory 500, window 80, threshold 0.28, 400 frames. Historical preset name; no remote-viewing validation.
coherence — 400 agents, threshold 0.26, decay 0.997, 300 frames.
dense-agents — 800 agents, 96×96 field, 200 frames.

perceiver, forecaster, and integrator currently label the same rolling Pearson detector. LAG_FRAMES, SAMPLE_PER_FRAME, and the three legacy moderator toggles do not alter the current engine; the passport lists these inactive settings. No lagged forecasting or distinct operator algorithm is claimed.

documents.title: IONS-X Deep Emergence Lab — Architecture
documents.text:
flowchart TD
 C["Configuration + seed"] --> E["Simulation engine"]
 T["Synthetic field or CSV telemetry"] --> E
 E --> O["Moving operators + rolling memory"]
 O --> G["Undirected association graph"]
 G --> R["Animation or JSON report"]
 E --> R

The ATOM framing organizes analyses, targets, operators, and moderators. The engine owns sequential state advancement; an explicit animation initializer prevents extra frame-zero steps, and duplicate requests for the current frame return its existing snapshot. Metrics, CSV records, and visualization therefore share one frame clock.

documents.title: IONS-X Deep Emergence Lab — Reproduce and contribute
documents.text:
python -m pip install -e '.[dev]'
python -m ruff check .
python -m pytest -q
python -m build

Tests compare real HTML and GIF execution against headless metrics, check exact frame counts and paired random schedules, and cover configuration isolation, empirical input rejection, provenance, and graph decay. CI runs Python 3.10–3.12, verifies the wheel build, and uploads rendered, headless, and paired-study smoke artifacts.

Reproducibility means matching scientific metrics for the same code, input, effective configuration, backend, and dependency environment. …

documents.title: James (topherchris420/james)
documents.text:
A desktop AI companion that runs on your computer and asks before it touches anything.

Chat with a model on your own machine. Show it your screen when you choose. Approve every click and keystroke before it happens.

Download · Getting started · What it can do · Privacy and safety · Status · Docs

A real session, not a mockup. James 0.4.0 on Linux with Gemma 3 4B in Ollama 0.40.3, on the same computer. The reply is the model's own, unedited. How this was captured.

James is a free, open-source desktop app, written in Rust by
Vers3Dynamics. It talks to an AI model that runs
on your own computer, through a model app such as LM Studio, Ollama, or
llama.cpp. It has no internet connection of its own, no account and no
analytics.

Most desktop agents ask for your trust up front and then act on it. James
works the other way round. The model can talk, look, and suggest as much as you
like, but it never holds the keys: anything that would change your computer is
one exact proposal that you inspect and approve once, and then James waits
while you check what happened.

Intelligence may propose. Evidence must be checked. Authority stays with the human.

Important: James 0.4.0 is a developer preview. Downloads are not code-signed.
Read what has and hasn't been verified before relying on it.

documents.title: James — What James can do
documents.text:
Guided setup — Five short steps from "what is this?" to a real answer: how to get LM Studio or Ollama for your system, finding your model app, a test message, and what screen capture and permissions mean. Resumes where you left off.
Chat — Replies stream in as the model writes them, with headings, lists, emphasis, and copyable code. Stop ends a reply at once and keeps what arrived, marked incomplete. Copy, Ask again, and Try again are one click away.
Know your model — James asks your model app what the model can do — read images, chat, its context window, whether it is loaded — and switches off features the model can't support, instead of letting them fail.
No silent cloud — If your model app says a model runs on another computer (Ollama's cloud models), James labels it, warns you, and never picks it for you.
Screen help — Guide me takes one picture of your screen, only when you press it, and suggests up to three next steps you take yourself. Turn on step numbers in Settings to have your model mark where each one is on the picture; small models often misplace them. Or capture, look at the preview, and attach it to a question. Needs a model that reads images.
Reviewed input (Windows) — James can press one key, click once or type text you approved after a five-second countdown, only if the window from your screenshot is in front. Then it waits for you to check the result.
Voice — Talk hands-free, dictate into the message box, or have answers read aloud. Listening runs on your computer. Voice can never approve an action.
R.A.I.N. Lab — A read-only view of R.A.I.N. Lab research: what the Lab is doing, recent simulator results labelled by how far they were checked, and, only if you turn it on, a short summary shared with your model.
Your preferences — Light, dark or system theme in Vers3Dynamics teal, high contrast, text from 80% to 200%, reduced motion, full keyboard control (F1 lists shortcuts) and screen-reader labels.

documents.title: James — Get started
documents.text:
1. Download James:

From the Releases page:

Your computer — Download
Windows 10 or 11, 64-bit — James--windows-x64-setup.exe (installs for your account, no admin password), or the …-portable.exe
Mac with macOS 11 or newer, Apple silicon or Intel — James--macos-universal.zip; drag James to Applications
Ubuntu 22.04+, Debian 12+, Linux Mint 21+ — james__amd64.deb
Other 64-bit Linux (glibc 2.35+) — James--linux-x86_64.tar.gz; run ./install.sh

The builds are not code-signed yet, so Windows SmartScreen and macOS
Gatekeeper warn the first time you open James; the
getting started guide shows how to
continue. To check a download, compare it with SHA256SUMS.txt, or verify its
build provenance with gh attestation verify --repo topherchris420/james.

2. Get a model app and a model:

James doesn't include a model. Install a free model app and download a model
— Gemma 3 4B is a good first choice: about 3 GB, runs on most computers with
8 GB of memory, and can read images:

- LM Studio: search for Gemma 3 4B, download and load it, then switch the server on in the Developer tab. No terminal needed.
- Ollama: install it, then get the model in the Ollama app (Windows and Mac) or with ollama pull gemma3:4b.
- llama.cpp's llama-server or any OpenAI-compatible server on your computer also works.

3. Open James and follow the setup:

James finds your model app, sends one test message, and explains screen
capture and permissions. The getting started guide
covers every step in plain language, with troubleshooting.

Run from source instead:

Install Rust 1.88 or newer and your platform's build tools (on Windows,
Visual Studio C++ Build Tools), then:

git clone https://github.com/topherchris420/james.git
cd james
cargo run -p james-desktop --release --locked

On Linux James also needs an OpenGL driver and libxkbcommon-x11-0. To check a
model server from a terminal on any system:

cargo run -p james-models --example probe -- ollama --chat "Say hello"

documents.title: James — Supported model apps
documents.text:
Model app — Default port — Verified
Ollama — 11434 — Real: 0.40.3 — chat, streaming, Stop, images, capabilities, cloud-model warning, errors
llama.cpp llama-server — 8080 — Real: b11564 — chat, streaming, images, capabilities, errors
LM Studio — 1234 — Protocol fixtures only; not yet run against real LM Studio
Other OpenAI-compatible servers — your choice — Fixtures; llama-cpp-python in an earlier session

James never installs software, downloads models, changes your model app's
settings or switches to another provider by itself.

documents.title: James — Privacy and safety
documents.text:
- Nothing leaves this computer through James. Every request goes through
 james-loopback, whose only address is a port on
 127.0.0.1. There is no hostname, DNS, proxy, redirect or update check.
 Your model app decides where the model runs; James tells you when it says
 "elsewhere".
- No background watching. A screenshot is taken only when you press
 Capture or Guide me, kept in memory, and sent to your model only when you
 attach it. Microphone audio is deleted as soon as it becomes text.
- Your data stays yours. Conversations and settings are saved in one
 folder that only your account can read (on macOS and Linux James sets this
 itself). Turn history off, clear a conversation, or delete everything in
 Settings → Privacy. Files are not encrypted; full-disk encryption
 protects them if your computer is lost.
- Every action is yours. On Windows, James performs at most one click, key
 or piece of text at a time, only after Allow once, only while the window
 from your screenshot is in front, never into James itself. It writes down
 what it is about to do first, and after a crash shows you exactly what that
 was and never repeats it. Stop or Esc cancels the countdown; input
 already sent cannot be undone. There is no shell, no file access and no
 action chain, and nothing a model writes can approve anything.

More detail: SECURITY.md and supervision.

documents.title: James — R.A.I.N. Lab
documents.text:
James is the desktop companion of R.A.I.N. Lab,
a simulated-city research environment. Start the Lab (npm ci && npm run dev),
open R.A.I.N. Lab in James and press Find the Lab.

James shows what the Lab is doing, each recent result as *supported / not
supported in the simulator*, whether it was replayed and registered, and
model-written hypotheses labelled as such. Lab results are simulator output,
not real-world evidence, and James treats them as material to discuss, never
as instructions. It cannot start, steer or approve anything in the Lab. See
the Lab guide.

documents.title: Luca (topherchris420/Luca)
documents.text:
Network traffic capture, indicator matching, and behavioral analysis for devices connected through a monitored Wi-Fi access point.

Luca observes network communications without installing an agent on the device being examined. It captures packets at a dedicated access point, processes them with Zeek and Suricata, and turns the results into structured findings and a PDF report.

The system is intended for authorized network inspection and research. A match or heuristic alert is evidence for investigation, not proof that a device is compromised.

documents.title: Luca — How it works
documents.text:
1. Connect: A phone or other Wi-Fi device joins the access point managed by Luca. An upstream interface supplies network connectivity.
2. Capture: TShark records TCP and UDP traffic from the configured capture interface to capture.pcap.
3. Analyze: Zeek extracts connection and protocol metadata; Suricata evaluates rules against the packet capture. The analysis coordinator starts the two engines as separate processes.
4. Correlate: Detection logic evaluates observed connections against indicators of compromise (IoCs), configured heuristics, and allowlists.
5. Report: Findings are grouped by severity and written alongside connection details and a generated PDF. Capture artifacts can be exported for further analysis.

The high-level data path is:

documents.title: Luca — Detection capabilities
documents.text:
Component — What it examines
Zeek — Connection records, DNS resolutions, HTTP metadata, and TLS/certificate metadata.
Indicator matching — Configured domains, IP addresses, CIDR ranges, name servers, dynamic-DNS providers, TLDs, and certificate fingerprints, where relevant metadata is available.
Behavioral heuristics — Protocol/port anomalies, unusual destinations, TLS certificate conditions, and other configurable signals implemented by the analysis engine.
Suricata — Network signatures stored as Snort-compatible rules plus contextual rules generated for a capture.
Allowlists — Known permitted hosts, addresses, and ranges used to reduce noisy findings.

Severity classifications are High, Moderate, and Low. The detection surface depends on what the device transmits, what remains observable through encryption, and the quality of configured intelligence.

documents.title: Luca — Architecture
documents.text:
Layer — Implementation — Source
User interface — Vue 2 capture, network setup, analysis, and report workflow — app/frontend/
Frontend API — Flask routes for network configuration, capture, analysis, device information, and exports — server/frontend/
Analysis engine — Python coordinator running Zeek and Suricata against saved PCAPs — analysis/
Administration — Vue 2 interface and Flask API for settings, IoCs, allowlists, and MISP integrations — app/backend/, server/backend/
Intelligence storage — SQLite tables for indicators, allowlist entries, and MISP connection settings — assets/scheme.sql
Feed synchronization — Background loaders for configured IoC/allowlist URLs and MISP instances — server/backend/watchers.py

Analysis artifacts:

A typical capture is stored in a token-specific directory under /tmp/. The pipeline uses or generates:

/tmp//
├── capture.pcap
└── assets/
 ├── alerts.json
 ├── conns.json
 ├── whitelist.json
 ├── device.json
 ├── capinfos.json
 └── report.pdf

The set of files depends on capture progress and whether each analysis stage completed. The frontend also supports exporting the capture directory as a ZIP, including via a removable USB device.

documents.title: Luca — Installation
documents.text:
Requirements: A Debian-family Linux system, root access for installation, an AP-capable Wi-Fi interface for the monitored device, and a separate upstream network interface. The install script provisions host networking and services, so use a dedicated machine, not your daily workstation.

git clone https://github.com/topherchris420/Luca.git
cd Luca
sudo bash install.sh

The installer interactively selects interfaces, creates the access-point configuration, installs system dependencies, builds both Vue applications, configures the database and systemd services, and generates a self-signed certificate for administration. Bundled indicator data is seeded locally; optional remote feeds can be configured later. Review install.sh before running it: it can modify DNS, hostname, DHCP, network forwarding, and system services.

Luca-native deployment: Installation uses /usr/share/luca, luca-* systemd services, and luca.local. Previously installed instances under other names require a migration or fresh installation; this release does not automatically migrate their databases.

After installation, the conventional local interfaces are:

Interface — Address — Purpose
Capture UI — http://luca.local — Configure the monitored connection, run a capture, review findings
Administration — https://luca.local — Manage configuration, IoCs, allowlists, and integrations

The administrative HTTPS certificate is self-signed. Hostname resolution and reachability depend on the machine's network configuration.

documents.title: Luca — Working with captures
documents.text:
Through the capture UI, select or configure the upstream connection, start the access point, connect the device under inspection, record a session, and run the analysis. Review the resulting severity-grouped alerts alongside the observed connections. Export evidence when needed.

The analysis pipeline can also be invoked against an existing capture directory containing capture.pcap on an installed and configured system:

python3 /usr/share/luca/analysis/analysis.py /path/to/capture-directory

The analyzer expects its dependencies, executable paths, indicator database, and configuration to have been provisioned.

documents.title: Luca — Configuration and intelligence
documents.text:
The main configuration is config.yaml.

Setting — Role
network.in / network.out — Capture-side and upstream network interfaces
analysis.heuristics / analysis.iocs — Heuristic and indicator-analysis controls
analysis.whitelist — Enable allowlist handling
analysis.max_alerts / analysis.max_ports — Detection thresholds
frontend.* / backend.* — User-interface behavior and service access
watchers.iocs / watchers.whitelists — External intelligence sources to load

The administration service supports adding and searching IoCs, adjusting allowlists, and configuring MISP sources. Optional external feeds are disabled by default; the watcher seeds the indicator database from the repository's bundled IoC and allowlist JSON. Feed accuracy and freshness affect detection quality. Evaluate external sources before trusting them.

documents.title: Luca — Technical limitations and operational security
documents.text:
- Traffic visibility is not endpoint visibility. Luca examines network evidence; it does not inspect installed apps, local files, or a device's memory.
- Encryption limits inspection. Metadata may remain observable, but encrypted application payloads are not automatically decrypted.
- Heuristics are probabilistic signals. Benign services can trigger alerts, and malicious traffic can evade available rules and indicators.
- Captures may contain sensitive data. Restrict access to PCAPs, exported ZIPs, reports, and the administration interface.
- The software uses legacy dependencies. Review and harden the Python, Vue, Node, and system package stack before exposing it beyond a controlled environment. In particular, review remote-access settings and the self-signed administrative certificate.
- Inspect only devices and networks you own or are authorized to assess.

documents.title: Luca — Updating Luca
documents.text:
The updater draws from Luca's repository. Because this repository may be private, sudo bash /usr/share/luca/update.sh requires Git credentials with access; if cloning fails, the installed application is left untouched. Remote version checks may be unavailable. Deployments using prior paths are not migrated automatically.

See LICENSE.txt and NOTICE.txt for license terms and third-party attributions.

documents.title: Nocturne (topherchris420/nocturne)
documents.text:
Light where it is needed. Darkness where it is not.

Nocturne is an open-source toolkit for reducing unnecessary light, starting with the controls people already have. DC Tonight turns an existing switch, timer or blind into a named-owner action, a calendar handoff and a record of what actually happened. Start with one building; coordinate the next willing neighbour.

For larger projects, set a sky-brightness target, compare changes across buildings, signs, sports fields and streetlights, and find the least-cost combination that meets the target under the conditions you specify.

A lit crossing does not need an illuminated sky. An occupied office does not need a glowing facade. Nocturne treats useful lighting and unwanted spill as separate things to account for: keep the service people need, then work backward from the night you want to restore.

Built by Christopher Woodyard / Vers3Dynamics, with Washington, DC as the worked example.

Research prototype · Python 3.10+ · MIT license. The planner (in a browser or on the command line), physics derivation, simulations, reports, integration checks and trial-analysis tools run today. Nocturne does not connect to a city's lighting system: contracts, equipment tests, safety reviews and the import itself remain deployment work, and the software records them rather than assuming them. DC results are model estimates; the restoration demonstrations use entirely invented data.

Do something tonight · Quick start · Restoration planner · Restoration example · DC estimates · Documentation

First real-world validation: One-building field pilot turns a consenting owner's reversible lighting change into a preregistered target/control experiment, with a manifest checked against the trial fingerprint. No owner has been recruited or physical result claimed in this repository. See the evidence ladder for what is modeled, self-reported, or measured.

documents.title: Nocturne — Do something tonight
documents.text:
The part we can address immediately is unnecessary light on property whose owner can act. A facade can stop glowing after closing. An occupied office can close its existing blinds. A closing checklist can include the dedicated decorative circuit. The people doing the work need a clear handoff and a way to record exceptions.

After the quick-start installation:

nocturne app --tonight

The local browser page lets you:

1. Add a switch/timer action, an existing blind, or an observation to route to an owner.
2. Name the responsible person, the specific circuit, the operating window, the useful lighting to preserve and the way to restore the previous setting.
3. Export an action sheet, a start-and-morning-check calendar, the project and an empty completion CSV.
4. Import the completed CSV to separate reported work, missed checks and actions needing review.

No new equipment is required for these first actions. Staff time and permission still matter. Every change is manual and reversible. Streetlights and federal assets become operator requests, never instructions to turn them off. DC Tonight links to Lights Out DC and the existing DDOT/311 service; a request can start today, while an actual repair may take much longer.

The distinction between planned and done is built into the accounting. A blank ledger claims no completed work. Unknown watts stay unquantified. Blinds get no electricity credit. A receipt must match the exact project and date; a service problem or replacement floodlight withholds credit pending review. Completion remains self-reported, and no circuit-level result is presented as measured citywide skyglow reduction.

Try the fictional example, or inspect its portable action sheet after downloading the repository:

nocturne tonight --example --date 2026-10-15 --out my-tonight-demo
# Open my-tonight-demo/action-sheet.html. The people and observations are invented.
nocturne receipts my-tonight-demo/project.json my-tonight-demo/receipts.csv
# Exit 3 is expected: the two owner-ready actions have no completion evidence yet.

For a real project, use Start fresh, record your own observations, and save the project before carrying out the agreed actions. Read the DC Tonight field guide for a first-night procedure, coordinated building routines and exact accounting rules.

documents.title: Nocturne — What you can do
documents.text:
Start with a question — Use Nocturne to…
What can I change tonight with the equipment already here? — Make owner action sheets, route spill reports, export calendar handoffs and reconcile completion receipts in DC Tonight.
Which changes would reach our darkness target? — Choose a portfolio across named owners, observation points and weather scenarios, within a budget and declared service constraints.
What if the target cannot be reached? — Identify a budget shortfall or show that the available actions are insufficient.
Will the plan hold in haze, under snow, or if our numbers are off? — Derive each source's effect from positions, lumens, shielding and the atmosphere; give uncertain values as ranges and plan for their pessimistic end; charge rebounds and synergies to the plans that trigger them.
Can one consenting building produce a defensible measured result? — Follow the first-site field protocol, preregister the randomized trial, run nocturne field-check on declared safety/measurement prerequisites, and analyze calibrated target/control readings.
Which sources contribute to the glow? — Design randomized source-isolation trials and analyze paired target/control observations.
Could existing streetlights use less energy? — Compare a year of electricity, cost and emissions under scheduled and adaptive lighting.
What happens during a network outage? — Simulate a lamp continuing to follow local rules after losing its connection.
Where does a fixture send its light? — Inspect IES photometry files for backlight, uplight and glare, and estimate light at a window.
How could a city coordinate a trial? — Export streetlight schedules, create a phased rollout, check crash data, and publish a shared Night Signal calendar.
Can our controllers actually run these schedules? — Check the schedules against each node family's declared limits (adapting them brighter-only), record contract, equipment and safety approvals against the exact files, and compare what the central system reports it loaded.

documents.text:
Download the repository through Code → Download ZIP, extract it, and open one of these files in your browser:

Derived-district report — The same kind of brief for a district whose coefficients were computed from geometry, haze and snow, with uncertainty ranges and a rebound.
Decision brief — Interactive estimates of energy costs, lighting through the night, modeled skies and the proposed rollout.
Operator console — A standalone browser demonstration of streetlight controller behavior.

GitHub displays HTML source at these links. Open the downloaded files locally to see the interfaces. These demonstrations do not connect to live lights.

documents.title: Nocturne — Quick start
documents.text:
You need Python 3.10 or newer. Git is optional if you download and extract the ZIP instead.

git clone https://github.com/topherchris420/nocturne.git
cd nocturne

macOS / Linux

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -e ".[dev]"

Windows PowerShell

py -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -e ".[dev]"

The Windows setup does not require script activation. In subsequent commands, replace nocturne with .\.venv\Scripts\nocturne.exe, and python with .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe.

The dev extra includes tests and chart generation. For the core command-line tools alone, install with python -m pip install -e ..

Plan in your browser:

nocturne app

This opens the planner in your browser. It runs on your computer only and sends nothing to lights. Start from an example or a blank project, then work through the tabs:

1. Places & targets: the observation points to protect and the most artificial sky brightness each may have.
2. Conditions: the nights the plan must work on, such as clear, hazy or snow.
3. Sources & options: each owner's lights and the complete changes they could make, with cost, service kept and effect.
4. Light contributions: how much each source adds at each place. Paste a block straight from a spreadsheet; type ranges such as 0.3 – 0.5 where a value is uncertain.
5. Plan: find the cheapest set of changes, then open the printable brief.

The panel on the right checks the project as you type and takes you to any field that needs fixing. To edit and save a file, start with it: nocturne app my-district.json. Save keeps the previous version as my-district.json.bak. Stop the planner with Ctrl+C in the terminal.
